subject: Environment
sub_topic: Tiger census methodology — camera trapping, pugmark, M-STrIPES

concepts.name: Pugmark Census Method: Historical Use and Scientific Limitations
key_dimensions: How pugmarks were used as the primary tiger identification tool pre-2006 and the role of trackers
Scientific criticism: inability to distinguish individual tigers, overestimation bias, and lack of reproducibility
Why the 2006 tiger census marked a formal shift away from pugmarks as the sole method
UPSC trap: Pugmarks are NOT fully abandoned — still used as supplementary field sign data in Phase I surveys

concepts.name: Four-Phase All India Tiger Estimation (AITE) Framework
key_dimensions: Phase I: Sign survey (pugmarks, scats, scrapes) at beat level by field staff
Phase II: Camera trapping at landscape level by WII-trained personnel
Phase III: Prey density estimation using line transect distance sampling
Phase IV: Habitat quality assessment using Remote Sensing and GIS — integration into final population estimate

concepts.name: Camera Trapping: Methodology and Individual Identification
key_dimensions: Use of bilateral stripe patterns (unique to each tiger like human fingerprints) for individual ID via camera trap photos
Capture-Mark-Recapture (CMR) statistical model used to estimate total population from camera trap data
Camera placement protocols: paired cameras at natural corridors, water holes, and pugmark-detected trails
UPSC trap: Camera trapping covers only a subset of tiger range (~30% of habitat); extrapolation methods used for rest

concepts.name: Capture-Mark-Recapture (CMR) Model in Tiger Estimation
key_dimensions: Statistical logic: ratio of marked (photographed) to unmarked individuals in recaptures estimates total population
Assumptions: population closure during sampling, equal catchability, no mark loss — sources of error
How occupancy models supplement CMR in areas with low camera trap density
Difference between CMR-based estimate and simple camera count — UPSC frequently tests this distinction

concepts.name: M-STrIPES: Design, Purpose, and Functionality
key_dimensions: Full form: Monitoring System for Tigers — Intensive Protection and Ecological Status
Developed by: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) in collaboration with National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)
Core function: Mobile app-based daily patrolling data entry by field guards — records GPS tracks, wildlife sightings, threats
Distinction from census: M-STrIPES is a continuous monitoring and anti-poaching tool, NOT a periodic census method

concepts.name: M-STrIPES vs. Camera Trapping: Functional Differences
key_dimensions: M-STrIPES = real-time, patrol-based, year-round monitoring; Camera trapping = periodic, intensive, population estimation
M-STrIPES data feeds into threat intelligence and ranger management; camera trap data feeds into population statistics
Both are mandated under the Revised Tiger Conservation Plan framework of NTCA
UPSC trap: M-STrIPES does NOT replace camera trapping for census — they serve complementary but distinct roles

concepts.name: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and NTCA: Roles in Census
key_dimensions: WII conducts the technical and scientific aspects of AITE — protocol design, data analysis, report publication
NTCA is the statutory body under Wildlife Protection Act (Amendment) 2006 that mandates and oversees the census
State Forest Departments execute field-level data collection under WII guidance
UPSC trap: WII is an autonomous institution under MoEFCC, not under NTCA — important institutional distinction

concepts.name: Occupancy Modelling and Habitat-Based Extrapolation
key_dimensions: Used to estimate tiger presence/density in areas not covered by camera traps using sign survey data
Covariates used: prey density, human disturbance index, vegetation type from NDVI/remote sensing
Connects Phase I (sign survey) data with Phase II (camera trap) data for landscape-level estimates
Critical for estimating tigers in Northeast India and Sundarbans where camera trapping is logistically difficult

concepts.name: India's Tiger Census Cycle and Publication History
key_dimensions: Census conducted every 4 years: 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 — following the Tiger Task Force recommendation
2022 census result: ~3,682 tigers (largest tiger population globally — ~75% of world's wild tigers)
2006 census was a watershed: introduced camera trapping, dropped exclusive reliance on pugmarks post-Sariska crisis
UPSC trap: The 4-year cycle is a convention, not a legal mandate under Wildlife Protection Act

concepts.name: Sariska Crisis (2004-05) and Its Impact on Census Methodology Reform
key_dimensions: Pugmark census had reported tigers in Sariska; ground verification revealed near-zero tiger presence — massive credibility failure
Triggered the formation of Tiger Task Force (2005) under Sunita Narain
Tiger Task Force recommended camera trapping and science-based monitoring — led to 2006 methodology overhaul
Institutional consequence: NTCA established under WPA Amendment 2006 as a direct response to census failure

concepts.name: Sundarbans Tiger Estimation: Unique Methodological Challenges
key_dimensions: Mangrove terrain makes camera trap installation and pugmark tracking extremely difficult
Alternative methods used: camera traps on floating platforms, virtual cameras, and sign surveys along tidal creeks
Population estimates for Sundarbans carry higher uncertainty ranges than dry forest reserves
Shared tiger population with Bangladesh — transboundary estimation coordination under Global Tiger Forum

concepts.name: Global Tiger Forum (GTF) and Tx2 Goal: International Census Context
key_dimensions: Tx2 Goal (2010): Doubling wild tiger numbers by 2022 — adopted at St. Petersburg Tiger Summit
India's 2022 census showing ~3,682 tigers positioned it as the country that contributed most to Tx2 achievement
GTF's role: coordinates tiger range country data sharing and standardizes monitoring protocols
UPSC trap: Tx2 was a voluntary commitment, not a legally binding treaty obligation

concepts.name: Line Transect Distance Sampling for Prey Density Estimation
key_dimensions: Phase III of AITE — estimates density of prey species (deer, wild pig, gaur) which determines tiger carrying capacity
Method: observers walk fixed transects, record perpendicular distances to prey sightings, modeled statistically
Prey density is a co-variable in occupancy models — low prey areas show lower tiger sign frequency
UPSC trap: Prey density estimation is part of the tiger census framework, not a separate standalone exercise

concepts.name: eDNA and Emerging Technologies in Tiger Monitoring
key_dimensions: Environmental DNA (eDNA) from water sources, scats — being piloted for non-invasive tiger detection
Acoustic monitoring and AI-based camera trap image analysis (e.g., ExtractCompare software for stripe ID)
Drone-based surveys being tested for open habitat tigers (e.g., Dudhwa)
Current status: these are supplementary/experimental — camera trapping remains the gold standard for UPSC purposes

concepts.name: Tiger Reserve vs. Tiger Landscape: Census Coverage Distinction
key_dimensions: Census covers all tiger-bearing forests — not just 53 Tiger Reserves but also corridors and non-PA forest areas
Tiger landscape concept: ~18 source populations identified across India that sustain metapopulation dynamics
Camera trapping is intensive inside Tiger Reserves; occupancy modelling used in buffer and corridor areas
UPSC trap: Headline census number includes tigers OUTSIDE protected areas — often misread as Tiger Reserve count only

concepts.name: Statistical Confidence Intervals and Uncertainty in Tiger Counts
key_dimensions: Official estimates are always reported with confidence intervals (e.g., 3,167–3,925 in 2022) — not exact counts
Sources of uncertainty: imperfect detection, camera trap spacing, model assumptions in occupancy analysis
Minimum viable population (MVP) concept: ~100 individuals needed for long-term genetic viability — relevant for small reserves
UPSC trap: Media often reports the central estimate as an exact figure; UPSC may test awareness of range-based reporting

concepts.name: Role of State Forest Departments and Beat Guards in Phase I Data Collection
key_dimensions: Beat guards (lowest field unit) collect Phase I sign survey data along fixed routes — forms the base of the pyramid
Training by WII essential: errors at Phase I propagate through the entire estimation model
M-STrIPES digitizes patrol data — reduces manual error and enables real-time monitoring by range officers
Human capacity gap: many Tiger Reserves report insufficient trained personnel for rigorous Phase I surveys

concepts.name: Transboundary Tiger Populations and Cross-Border Census Coordination
key_dimensions: Key transboundary landscapes: India-Nepal (Terai Arc), India-Bhutan (Eastern Himalayas), India-Bangladesh (Sundarbans)
Tigers move across borders — double counting risk if censuses are conducted independently
Protocols: coordinating camera trap deployment dates and grid alignment along international borders
Global Tiger Recovery Program (GTRP) framework facilitates data sharing among 13 tiger range countries

concepts.name: NTCA's Annual Report and Monitoring Obligations under WPA 2006
key_dimensions: Section 38O of WPA 1972 (as amended 2006): mandates NTCA to ensure tiger conservation and monitoring
NTCA issues Tiger Conservation Plan approval — monitoring methodology compliance is a condition
Annual Status of Tigers in India reports vs. quadrennial AITE census — different periodicity and scope
UPSC trap: NTCA has advisory and regulatory powers but enforcement (anti-poaching operations) rests with State governments

concepts.name: Comparison: India's Tiger Census vs. African Wildlife Census Methodologies
key_dimensions: Africa uses aerial surveys (for large open savannahs) — not applicable to India's dense forest cover
India's CMR + occupancy model approach is considered globally more rigorous for elusive forest species
IUCN Red List assessments for tigers rely significantly on India's WII-NTCA methodology as the reference standard
Snow leopard and leopard censuses in India are adapting the same camera trap + occupancy framework — methodology transfer
